en: Preface to the *Vajra-Right-Eye*:
The Elder Śākyamuni has revealed his entire being and turned everything over from its very depths, pointing directly to what is present before us.

His intent is to demonstrate that the daily activities of all sentient beings are equal to those of the Buddha, so as to cause them to see through to their own minds and realize Prajñā, thereby beholding it for themselves.
The Dharma-body is primordially present; the entire body is a mirror, and the entire body is the mind. It is neither form nor mind; it is both mind and form.
In every instance there is the sublime, and in every matter there is the true. Yet, ultimately, it returns to the fact that there is no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, its unfolding and rolling up are without fixed pattern, its concealment and manifestation are unknowable, as it radiates brilliance.

Embracing emptiness, it is vast and eternally quiescent; there is nothing that does not flow forth from within the breast. Thus, one is able to act with sovereign freedom in all directions, wielding both destruction and life as the occasion demands.
This is beyond the reach of discursive thought and conceptual discrimination. To hesitate or doubt is to cause the soul to tremble with terror;

to engage in deliberation is for the dust of worldly toil to arise first. Applying oneself according to circumstances and responding to things without a fixed mind, one transcends the supernatural powers of the six swift steeds.
Reaching the subtle profundity of the ultimate pivot, one crosses the torrent like a fragrant elephant, cutting through the current; how marvelous!
The coarseness of attachment to self is entirely dispelled, and the subtlety of attachment to phenomena is completely melted away.

There is no Buddha to be realized, no Dharma to be taught, no Bodhi to be attained, no beings to be delivered, and no lands to be adorned. Only in this way does one behold the true Buddha of one’s own mind.
Thus we know that the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born are all the entire bodies of the Buddhas;
their scales, shells, feathers, and fur are entirely the Dharma-realm of Vairocana. Conceived within form yet not obscured, they equalize the myriad existences within the Great Void.
It is only because the mind cannot remain pure that one must sever the flight of discursive consciousness and cut through the nesting holes of doubt, dwelling no longer in sounds.
Fragrance, flavor, and touch are as tranquil as the four directions of space; they are luminously and uniquely revealed, illuminating the subtle mysteries of all phenomena.
Vast, penetrating, and spiritually brilliant, one recognizes that the three minds are non-different—like sparks struck from stone, like flashes of lightning.

Thus, within the ordinary mind one perceives the Buddha-mind; within conventional truth one clarifies ultimate truth. Worldly dharmas are themselves Buddha-dharmas; Buddha-dharmas are themselves worldly dharmas.

This is the way of the world. Who is not a Buddha? Who is a sentient being? To recognize the Buddhas among those with horns and fur, and to transform the holy and the profane within the cauldrons and furnaces—only when one shares the same nostrils as the Buddhas of the three periods can one know that there is no Buddha to be realized, no beings to be saved, and no lands to be adorned.
Thus, the Buddha is the sentient being, and the sentient being is the Buddha. Defilement is...
It is not defilement; it is adornment yet not adornment. Nevertheless, while it is not difficult to realize [this], it is difficult to empty the mind.
When practice and understanding are perfected and the profound comes forth without obstruction, one has made progress beyond the tip of the pole.
Only after such realization and refined study does one come to know that for forty-nine years, the Elder Śākyamuni never spoke a single word.
Written in the eighth month of autumn in the Gengwu year of the Chongzhen era at the Qiansong Chan Temple on Mount Bian.
Recorded by Ming Qiansong, the Eye of the True Vajra. Notes.
Now, the discourse on the Dharma of Prajñā is the true essence of all Buddhas, the true cause of the *dharmatā*, and the life-force of wisdom for all sentient beings.
Therefore, the World-Honored One first revealed this true essence to sentient beings so that it might serve as a constant reminder within the very tools of daily life;
the *dharmakāya* is no different from this, and it is thus for all that stirs. This clarifies that the true mark is not...
To distinguish between the noble and the ordinary, the Tathāgata spoke this Dharma for the sake of worldly people;
yet they are like the *kṣīrika* insects or the frogs in a pit, no longer knowing that there is a reality beyond.

Therefore, the World-Honored One directly points to the fundamental local radiance beneath one’s own heels—where there has never been any leakage—and which is equal to the Buddha, vividly alive and dynamically flowing.
At that moment, one suddenly sees through it all; only then does one realize that the ultimate and the conventional are of one essence, and that even the wriggling insects possess it.
Thus, within the circumstances and conditions of daily life—the very "tactics and lures"—one must personally examine for oneself: what principle is this? What kind of realm is this?
Whose activity is this? Whose nostrils are these? When one attains such mastery and becomes as fluid and unimpeded as a spinning wheel, [the Way is realized].
Vibrant and surging, it is released and gathered back with total freedom and spontaneity, without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort. It is the functioning of the whole body;
there is nothing that does not manifest as it is, and nothing that is not revealed as it is. Because it is thus, the entire body of all Buddhas is manifested;
because it is thus, the great wisdom of all Buddhas is revealed. Because all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*), it is called "Thus" (*tathā*). Because it is thus...
Therefore, the World-Honored One immediately donned his robes, took up his bowl, entered the city to beg for food, washed his feet, spread out his seat, and showed it to them, saying:
"This is what people use in the present; you may take it as a model to remind yourself. Look directly beneath your own heels;

you must thoroughly penetrate the World-Honored One’s method of application, and by doing so, you will recognize your own method of application. There is nothing particularly marvelous about the World-Honored One."
Specifically, one is able to recognize this which, from beginningless kalpas, has never been subject to decay; it is called the adamantine indestructible body (*vajra-akṣaya-kāya*).
It is the true mark that is neither born nor extinguished. When the world is destroyed, this does not perish. Because it is like gold, it does not change color;
because it is like adamant (*vajra*), it is not destroyed even when smelted. Therefore, its true nature is likened to the *vajra*.
Because it does not depart from the daily activities of sentient beings, the World-Honored One, within the midst of daily life, reminds all people;
this serves as the introduction to its arousal. When Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) saw the skillful means employed by the World-Honored One, he said, "The World-Honored One is rare indeed."
This is not a phenomenon obtainable within the world, nor is it a characteristic of permanence within the world; therefore, it is called "rare.
To recognize this is to understand that it is not a worldly dharma. However, [Subhūti] asks regarding those who have resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*:
"World-Honored One, how should this bodhicitta be established? How should it be subdued?"
Therefore, one who guards their mindfulness should abide accordingly; one who is able to recognize their mindfulness has achieved subjugation.
For this reason, the ten classes of sentient beings are all led into *nirvāṇa* without remainder and brought to liberation. Yet, in truth, there are no sentient beings who attain liberation.
One must realize that when the World-Honored One puts on his robes, takes up his bowl, enters the city for alms, washes his feet, and spreads his seat, [he acts thus].
Such is the true reality of *nirvāṇa*. One who can awaken to this reality attains true entry into extinction and truly achieves *nirvāṇa*.

This is the true emptiness of the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*). It is the true subduing [of delusion]. Throughout the two periods of six hours (*ṣaṭ-ṣaṭ-kāla*) of every day, all sentient beings do not depart from their own habitual self-use;
yet within the midst of daily life, such a person is able to personally shoulder the burden of the Tathāgata. When one truly realizes and truly awakens, then as for the four marks—
They are empty; they are truly in extinction (*parinirvāṇa*). Nevertheless, their various forms arise according to the human mind, and the mind revolves according to karma.

Thus, ignorance constitutes egg-birth; being enveloped by afflictions constitutes womb-birth; being moistened by the waters of craving constitutes moisture-birth; and the sudden arising of afflictions constitutes transformation-birth.
Because one’s own mind has not yet become empty and the notions of self and person have not yet been purified, these ten classes of forms follow the mind and its karma.
Although the forms manifested differ, the mind remains unchanged; therefore, all that stirs and moves manifests the true reality of nirvana.

Because one is able to awaken to this for oneself, the wise transcend the unformed from the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*). This unformed mind is empty in every thought-moment; this is called "delivering sentient beings.
In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain deliverance. This is the true realization of the essence of nirvana.

It is devoid of the marks of arising and ceasing; devoid of the marks of past and present; devoid of the marks of sage and ordinary person; devoid of the marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span;

and likewise devoid of the mark of nirvana. All possess the true essence. If one perceives that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata, for the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is without dualistic marks.
It manifests its profound root beyond all phenomena, equalizing the myriad existences within the Great Void. Not...
It can be attained through form and name alone. Yet when Cook Ding observes it, he no longer sees the ox as a whole.
This clarifies that there is nothing beyond *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) above; the method for entering extinction is thus made clear.
Prajñā, the true wisdom, is not the same as its essence and function; therefore, they must not be confused. To elucidate *prajñā* is precisely the great wisdom of all Buddhas.
That which sentient beings use daily without realizing is the samādhi of speech. It is like the sword of the Vajra King and like a great mass of fire;
therefore, it is called "unabiding generosity. When giving, there is no fixed point, for speech is free from contention; thus, the three spheres are empty and quiescent.
The four marks are all empty, and there is no fixed mark. It does not abide in sound, fragrance, taste, or touch; it is like the four directions of space.
When spiritual transformations arise—like the rushing of lightning and thunder—how could they be subject to deliberation?

Can they be grasped as phenomena, categorized as the stages of the worthy and sages, ranked among the four fruits of the path, or debated in terms of existence and non-existence? Like a raft in the middle of a river, how could they ever be an obstruction?
One must not become confused about the fundamental principle by following the literal phrasing, nor attempt to conjecture through verbal speculation;
such is not the Tathāgata’s true teaching, so how could it be the genuine essence of Prajñā?

Therefore, although the teachings are transmitted through words and phrases, one who can simply believe this single thought has planted various roots of goodness under millions of Buddhas and has attained such immeasurable merit.
One attains Buddhahood in a single instant precisely because one is able to believe that one’s own mind is the Buddha.
For the Buddha is speech, and speech is the mind; thus, when the mind manifests, speech follows swiftly, and as speech flows forth, the Buddha is perceived.
Consequently, adornment is non-adornment, and within all marks one perceives the markless; within sentient beings one perceives the non-sentient. Thus, one sees as suchness.
Have you come with a pure mind that dwells nowhere? Do you see the Tathāgata in the thirty-two marks, or in words that are not fixed?
For this reason, some give gifts of jewels as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; some give the gift of their body and life during the three periods of the day;
some say that one sees the Tathāgata through the thirty-two marks; and some [seek] for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi...
Because of the mind of *samyaksambodhi*; because of a body like that of Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains; because of the fact that all atoms are not atoms;
because of the teaching that the world is not a world; because of the fact that being free from all marks is itself called the Buddha;
and because of the fact that wherever one upholds, maintains, reads, or recites [the teachings], it is all the Sūtra—such were the various transformed sounds.
These various spiritual transformations are unfathomable in their function; they are not transformations produced by speech, but are the manifestation of the Buddhas' minds.
The mind is that which the Buddha reveals. When revealed, the Buddha has no abode. That which manifests while having no abode is the Buddha’s true Dharma-body, the true Dharma of Prajñā.
Therefore, it is like a flash of lightning, a spark from flint, or the Vajra-king sword.

It cannot be conjectured; it cannot be conceptualized. To dwell [in such thoughts] is to engage in conceptualization and deliberation, whereby the true essence of the *dharmatā* is cut and dismembered.
Thus, the true body of all Buddhas is wounded. Therefore, one must not allow false conceptualization to arise.
If it arises, one flows into birth and death and is no longer a seer of patience (*kṣānti*). Thus, the Tathāgata alone...
It is a manifestation and illumination; it is the teaching that dharmas have no reality and that words have no underlying principle.

It is to speak while remaining detached from the marks of letters and detached from the marks of mental objects. Therefore, "one" is immediately "not one"; as soon as something is spoken, it is swept away.

Dharmas have no marks of meaning, and speech has no fixed definition. As the ancient masters said: "If there were a real dharma to give to people, the grass before the Dharma Hall would be a foot deep."
Therefore, when one perceives the nature of all Buddhas within true speech and reality, all karmic offenses from previous lives can be completely extinguished. Why is this?
The essence of that nature is like empty space. Where in empty space could cauldrons of boiling water, furnaces of burning coals, mountains of blades, or forests of swords be established?
It is simply that people are unable to awaken to their own nature in every word and every movement.
[The interlocutor] considers his own true nature to be the indestructible reality.
However, if a person has not yet awakened and their self-nature is not yet empty, one cannot say they are free from sinful karma.

Therefore, the merit of encountering Buddhas for as many *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* as there are grains of sand in the Ganges cannot adorn the nature of emptiness; for emptiness cannot be made empty, and emptiness cannot be adorned. Only...
By means of the teaching of non-abiding, one can adorn empty space. For this reason, Śūnyatā-sambhava asked again, his doubts still not fully resolved:

"If there is the teaching of non-abiding, how should one abide and subdue [the mind]? Thus, the Tathāgata said, "I have brought all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, yet in reality, no sentient being has attained parinirvāṇa.
Although the Dharma has been explained, they have not yet awakened; though their minds desire awakening, [they remain unawakened].
One is able to be empty; both person and phenomena are forgotten, and both self and others are purified. That which the mind realizes is difficult;

after realization, it is difficult for the notions of self and others to remain unpurified. If the mind has already realized, and that realization is itself empty, then there remains only the non-self-mind responding to the world.
The words of non-self follow conditions; one does not perceive a dharma of nirvana, nor is there a mind of nirvana. Therefore, as such...
Coming from within the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, one extracts the *dharmatā* of all Buddhas; this is called possessing the *dharma-cakṣus*.
It is said that while it consists of words, it is not merely words; this is called the *prajñā-cakṣus*.

Being able to observe the bodies of sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, such that their true essence is fully revealed in a single utterance, is called the *divya-cakṣus*. Being able to observe the Buddhas of the three periods of time...

They do not enter extinction; rather, they are fully endowed with the true nature of *nirvāṇa* while manifesting in the *samādhi* of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). This is called the Buddha-eye. It is the Buddha and it is the Deva;

it is the Dharma and it is Wisdom. All of these emit light from the gateway of the faces of all sentient beings, illuminating each so that they may behold the inexhaustible manifestations of supernatural powers (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) flowing forth. These are words of truth, words of reality, and words of suchness. Not...
Deception is not falsehood; this is called the fleshly eye. For this reason, there is no past mind and no future mind; each exists only in the present.
One cannot perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks, nor can one see his characteristics through a complete physical body.
Furthermore, there is no dharma that can be preached, all for the sake of awakening the life-force of wisdom in sentient beings. Moreover, there are no sentient beings [to be found].
[He] transcends. One cannot seek [the Tathāgata] through sounds or forms; there is no name of "Bodhisattva" to be found, and no merit to be received.
It is only by means of non-self that one achieves patience (*kṣānti*). One cannot see the Tathāgata through walking, standing, sitting, or reclining.
Even the mark of a mote of dust is not the world, nor can one obtain a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span. All [these]...
This mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* cannot be viewed in such a way, nor can it be characterized by such marks.
Although it is said to be unmoving and suchness (*tathatā*), it is likewise an illusion, a dream, a bubble, or a shadow; it is like lightning or dew. Even "Buddha" is merely a name.
These words concerning the spiritual transformations of this sutra constitute the true cause of Prajñā. It is through these five phrases alone that [it is] the Tathāgata.
The true Dharma is revealed herein; yet for the observer, there is no place to apply the hand. This is precisely the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-kośa).
For this reason, it is designated by the name "the Right Eye."
